# Lever Espresso Machine

## Overview

I run a single group spring lever machine in the kitchen, bought used from a cafe that had replaced it with something volumetric. The group is a heavy commercial casting, and the lever on top of it is the only control that matters once the boiler is up to pressure. A pump machine gives you a flat nine bar curve and lets you forget about it, whereas the lever gives you a curve that rises and then fades as the spring relaxes, and you learn to read the flow by eye rather than by the gauge. The boiler is a small copper tank with an element and a sight glass, heated by a thermostat that I check against a thermometer once a month. Warm up takes about twenty minutes from cold, and I use that time to grind and to warm the cups on top of the group. The footprint is smaller than I expected, since the whole machine is a tall box with a lever sticking out of the front. I like the ritual of pulling the lever far more than I like pressing a button, and the shots have a softness to them that I have not managed to get from a pump.

## Setup

Getting the machine home was the first job, and it took a full weekend. I hired a small van and drove to the cafe on a Monday when it was closed, and we crated the machine with the lever removed and strapped down flat so it would not swing in transit. The boiler had been drained the day before, and even so the crate came out heavier than either of us expected, which meant a two person lift up a narrow stair and through a doorway I had measured twice. Once it was inside I set it on a bench I had built to suit it, with the top of the drip tray at 900 mm so that the lever falls comfortably to hand, and I cut a slot in the bench top for the drain hose rather than let it loop up where it could trap water. The plumbing was the fiddly part. The machine wants a soft supply line and no more than about 2 bar of mains pressure, so I fitted a small pressure reducer and a shut off valve under the bench, and I ran the waste into a tundish so I can see if anything is draining slowly.

Power came next, because the element draws a fair load and I did not want it sharing a circuit with the kettle. There is a 1400 W element in the boiler and a dedicated spur with its own breaker, which has not tripped once in three years. I filled the boiler through the supply, watched the sight glass climb to the mark, and then dry ran the lever a few times with the machine cold to feel the spring and the cam. The spring was stiffer than I expected and the lever pin had a dry squeak, so I put a smear of food safe grease on the pivot and worked it in. I checked the piston seals before the first real shot, since a machine that has sat idle in a cafe for a month can have seals that have gone flat, and they looked sound enough to use.

Water filtration matters more than anything else on a machine like this, so the supply runs through a small filter cartridge that I change on the calendar rather than by taste. The drip tray drains to the waste, the cups live on the warming tray, and the group sits above a stainless grate that I lift out for cleaning. I keep a thermometer clipped to the group so I can watch what the metal is doing rather than guessing from the boiler reading, and that thermometer is the single most useful thing I have added.

Dialling in is a slower business than on a pump machine. I started with the basket the machine came with and weighted my doses from the beginning, because a lever is far less forgiving of a bad puck than a pump, and an uneven bed will show up as a spray of water off the side of the group rather than a tidy stream. The grind sits a little coarser than I would use on a pump machine, since the pre-infusion does some of the work that a high pressure pump would do on its own.

I clean the group between bags, wipe the tray most days, and let the machine come up to pressure before I touch the lever. The supply filter, the drain and the thermometer all earn their place, and the bench height I chose on the first day still feels right every time I reach for the lever. I have also learned to leave the lever resting on its stop rather than parking it half raised, because a spring left under load will creep over time and lose the pressure curve I rely on. The machine gets a water only flush at the end of each session and a fuller clean of the group and the tray once a week, which keeps the piston seals supple and the grate free of old grounds. The portafilter and the basket are soaked in hot water rather than detergent, and everything is dried before it goes back on the machine.


The routine that has settled in is this. Pre-infusion runs about eight seconds while the group fills before the spring takes over, and I watch the first drops appear just as the lever starts to move. The boiler pressure sits at 1.1 bar, which is enough for steam and stable enough that the brew does not swing about. My standard dose is 15 g in, 35 g out, which suits the medium roasts I buy and gives me a repeatable cup. If the group has idled more than 20 minutes, I run a cooling flush before the shot, and after that flush the group thermometer reads 92 C, which is where I want it. That cooling flush is the habit that improved my results more than any change to the grinder.
## Maintenance

The piston gasket and the seals want changing every 18 months, and I do it whether or not they look tired, because a weeping seal shows up as water in the wrong place long before it fails outright. I keep a set of spares in the drawer with the food safe grease. The lever pin gets a drop of lubrication at the same service, and the cam and the roller get a light smear so the pull stays smooth. I check the sight glass for scale once a year and run a weak descale only if the glass looks cloudy, since a clean glass is a good sign that the boiler is not furring up. The group gets a back flush with water only, never detergent, because a lever has no three way valve to rinse the residue away. Nuts and fittings get a look at every service, and I re-tighten anything that has worked loose.

## Troubleshooting

Water coming out of the group when the lever is raised, before the puck is even loaded, almost always means a perished group gasket or a worn piston seal rather than a fault in the boiler. If the boiler overfills and the sight glass climbs past the mark, the level probe or the inlet valve is letting water in when it should not, and the fix is a new probe or a clean of the contacts. A bitter first shot after a long idle is the group sitting too hot, and it clears with the cooling flush I described above, so I now flush out of habit rather than waiting to taste the problem. A lever that drops on its own without pressure behind it points at a tired spring, and a rebuild kit is the proper cure. Strange noises at the group usually come from the piston seals running dry, so grease the cylinder walls at the next service.
